description.narrative:
The FAO-European Union Forest Law Enforcement, Governance and Trade (FLEGT) programme was a global demand-driven small grants mechanism funded in a Multi-donor trust fund by the European Union, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida). Sida contributed a total of SEK 75 million during the third phase of the programme, spanning from 2015 to 2021.
The programme was designed to provide technical support and resources for activities to further the goals of the European Unions FLEGT Action Plan, helping tropical timber-producing countries to establish and implement measures to tackle illegal logging, promoting trade in legal timber products and, ultimately, contributing to sustainable forest management (SFM) and poverty reduction. The programme delivered results towards five Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs); #1 Life on land, #2 Zero Hunger, #10 Reduced Inequalities, #12 Responsible Consumption and Production and #15 Life on land.
FAO provided support to the negotiation and implementation of voluntary partnership agreements (VPAs), bilateral trade agreements on legal timber trade between tropical timberproducing countries and the European Union. In countries not engaged in a formal VPA process, the programme supported measures to improve law enforcement, timber legality assurance and overall forest sector governance. The programme funded projects created by governments, civil society and private sector organizations in Latin America, Africa and Asia to improve forest governance and promote trade in legal timber products on domestic and international markets. The programme endorsed 375 projects in 27 countries and had a total budget of USD 50 584 350. The greatest investment was made in VPA countries, representing 73 percent of the budget, while 18 percent of the budget was invested in other tropical timber-producing countries, with the remainder supporting global and regional work.
Specifically, the programme pursued six primary outcomes:
Outcome 1: VPAs contribute to improved forest sector governance and timber legality on domestic and international markets.
Outcome 2: Initiatives that support legal production and consumption of timber and better forest sector governance in countries that are not engaged in the VPA process are strengthened.
Outcome 3: The capacity of the private sector to participate in the production, marketing and trade of legal timber has increased.
Outcome 4: Stakeholders in both consumer and producer countries demonstrate an improved knowledge of benefits from legal logging, international trade requirements and of best practices for FLEGT
Outcome 5: The progress, achievements and impacts of the FLEGT Action Plan are better understood and information is made available through an updated, robust and user-friendly information system.
Outcome 6: Increased technical and institutional capacities of service providers
The contribution has spun over several strategies and their goals. Ultimately, it contributed mainly to the following strategy goals in the Strategy for Swedens global development cooperation on sustainable economic development 20222026:
Strategy goal 4 (SG4): Improved conditions for sustainable and inclusive international trade
Strategy goal 5 (SG5): Improved conditions for food security, sustainable food systems, increased productivity and sustainability in agriculture, forestry and fishing, and strengthened ownership and tenure rights to land and natural resources
Strategy goal 3 (SG3): Improved conditions for sustainable and inclusive market and private sector development, and sustainable business
The programme has generated results on all results channels that the unit for global sustainable economic development work with; global and normative changes [GLOB/NORM], national and institutional changes [NAT/INST] and changes for the target group [ACT/TARGET].

Det föreslagna programmet har som målsättning att uppnå en god styrning av skogsbruket i utvecklingsländer samt att främja legal handel med skogsprodukter. Detta förväntas även på lång sikt bidra till en hållbar skogsanvändning och fattigdomsbekämpning. FAO FLEGT är ett stödprogram till EU FLEGT, för att bygga kunskap och kapacitet på policy- såväl som på företags- och samhällsnivå för att länder ska kunna ingå i ”voluntary partnership agreements” (VPA) förhandlingar och/eller för att kunna förbereda och verkställa initiativ för hållbart skogsbruk utanför VPA ramverket. Det är en utveckling av tidigare fas av samma program men med ett större fokus på små och medium-stora företag och deras möjlighet att påverka och delta i förhandlingar om skogslagstiftning och legal handel. Sidas bedömning är att insatsen har potential till att bidra till ett mer hållbart skogsbruk (miljömässigt, socialt och ekonomiskt) och till att de potentiella fördelarna med legal handel av timmer och handelsavtal för ett hållbart skogsbruk även gagnar småbrukare och har potential att hjälpa människor ur fattigdom.
Programmets totala budget är 45,000,000 USD (ca 332,300,000 SEK) av vilket FAO själv kommer att bidra med 10% av Sidas och ECs bidrag. EC har initialt gått in med 13,000,000 EUR men förväntas öka sitt bidrag i takt med att programmet implementeras. Cirka hälften av budgeten kommer att vidareförmedlas i form av grants genom en direkt stöd mekanism och årliga ”call for proposals” i de aktuella länderna (15 VPA länder och 10 icke-VPA länder).
Initiativet styrs och genomförs av FAO som har stor teknisk kunskap i området samt lång erfarenhet av liknande initiativ till exempel National Forest Program Facility (NFP) och Forest and Farm Facility (FFF). Sida stödjer redan FFF initiativet med ett kärnstöd över fem år och FLEGT Facility regionalt (Asien). Det finns goda möjligheter till synergier mellan de tre programmen och Sida, i sin roll som betydande givare till båda, har möjligheten att bidra till utvecklingen mot ett globalt hållbart skogsbruk.

The FLEGT (Forest Law Enforcement, Governance and Trade) initiative aims to exclude illegal timber from the markets, to improve the supply of legal timber and to increase the demand for responsible wood products. The initiative will lead to a positive impact, economic as well as social, in the areas of intervention.

The results of the programmes is presented by outcome area below. It has also been indicated which strategy goal and result channel the result is mainly contributing to. Most of the results below are extracted from the final evaluation, assessed as the most independent source of information, triangulating the conclusions buy using an array of sources such as FAO reports, surveys, case studies and interviews.
Results per outcome area
Outcome 1: VPAs contribute to improved forest sector governance and timber legality on domestic and international markets
Outcome 1 covers 15 VPA countries, representing around 73 percent of the Programmes total budget. Of these, three countries (Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Malaysia) had lower levels of engagement due to a slowdown or halting of VPA processes, while the other 12 (Cameroon, Central African Republic, Congo, Côte dIvoire, Ghana, Guyana, Honduras, Indonesia, Lao Peoples Democratic Republic, Liberia, Thailand and Viet Nam) featured robust portfolios. Some of the most significant results under outcome 1 include:
- Increased legality and traceability including monitoring of timber products. Monitoring was done thogh data management and monitoring, for example though digital tools and the Timber Legality Assurance System (TLAS). The basic idea of timber traceability is to ensure that the origin and sustainble cutting of the timber was done, taking sustainable forestry management into account. Legality improved throgh legal and policy changes, e.g. defining legality and procurement policies. The tools developed for transparency, legality and the systems development for improved legal compliance, has triggered more traceability (data management and monitoring) and legal and policy changes (e.g. defining legality, procurement policies) for improved legality overall. SG4 [NAT/INST] [GLOB/NORM]
- In Malaysia, the Harmonised Reduced Impact Logging Guidelines were compiled, subjected to multistakeholder consultation and incorporated into the State Forestry Ordinance. In Ghana, technical support enabled the Government to secure stakeholder inputs in the revised guidelines for plantation timber harvesting, which will improve profitability and sustainable practices in the plantation timber industry, as well as unblocking the adoption of timber legality requirements in public procurement processes. In Côte dIvoire, five decrees for implementing the Forest Code were produced and presented to the Ministry for Water and Forests. In Honduras, the Programme contributed to improved regulations to facilitate tenure regularization processes in national forest areas under community management. SG4, SG5 [NAT/INST]
- One of the principal aspects of forest governance that was supported by FLEGT was a more inclusive and transparent debate between civil society, public and private stakeholders. This was achieved through the establishment of multi-stakeholder platforms that were set up to support VPA negotiations. What can be credited to the programme here, is that the people who sit in the private sector college of the technical negotiating committee could integrate representative of small operators and that the debates did not concern only the big industries. Small operators have had the opportunity to be involved in the implementation and feedback of the various projects, or in the validation of certain project proposals. SG3, SG4, SG5 [NAT/INST]
-Independent forest monitoring (IFM) was strengthened in many VPA countries. IFM was supported through projects in the Central African Republic, Côte DIvoire, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gabon, Ghana, Guyana and Indonesia and produced 140 independent monitoring reports. Six projects successfully activated government response to irregularities. In Indonesia, the programme supported six partners to expand the reach of independent monitoring activities and improve the capacities of around 800 independent forest monitors, including 98 members of indigenous communities in provinces across six islands. In the Central African Republic, FLEGT support to IFM by local civil society organizations (CSOs) led to successful verification missions by the forestry administration. As a result, four national CSOs were trained, three IFM missions were conducted, six IFM reports were produced and reviewed by the national committee. SG4, SG5 [NAT/INST]
- The programme has made significant progress in VPA countries on developing and implementing elements of TLAS. In Honduras, FLEGT support to both the public Institute for Forest Conservation and private sector organizations resulted in the development and adoption of the Honduras TLAS, and training of smallholders agroforestry producers and MSME to comply. The Honduras TLAS is based on the countrys existing national strategy against illegal logging, IFM and the digital traceability system. In Côte dIvoire, the definition of legality is now underway, as is the TLAS. In Ghana, draft guidelines for plantation timber harvesting have been developed based on the Ghana legality assurance system and requirements and conversion factors for plantation timber have been developed. In Indonesia, the core mechanism that has enabled FLEGT recognition is a state driven TLAS. SG4, SG5 [NAT/INST]
Outcome 2: Initiatives that support legal production and consumption of timber and better forest sector governance in countries that are not engaged in the VPA process are strengthened.
Outcome 2 focuses on support in countries willing to engage in FLEGT-related processes but not engaged in the VPA process. In the supported non-VPA countries there is an effective commitment to improved forest governance and timber legality and a demand for support to coordinated, multistakeholder initiatives. Initially, work started in six non-VPA countries but the scope was broadened to twelve countries. There was a large difference in support to non-VPA countries: where Colombia, Guatemala and Peru received between USD 630 000 and USD 940 000 for more than 15 projects per country according to a well-developed roadmap, others (e.g. Benin, Panama, Papua New Guinea, Cambodia) received a fraction of this (USD 34 000 - USD 192 000) for a few projects.
The 2020 annual report shows that all four indicators of outcome 2 have been achieved to a certain degree, particularly in the revisions of policy and legal frameworks (done in Peru, the Philippines and Myanmar), traceability systems (operational in Benin and Panama; initiated in Guatemala), multi stakeholder platforms and additional funding was leveraged to address issues identified in the country roadmap in Colombia and Peru. While these are relevant achievements, they are scattered over the four countries with higher amounts of projects (Peru, Colombia, Guatemala and the Philippines) and no contributions to outcome 2 indicators were reported for several non-VPA countries (Papua New Guinea, Madagascar, Uganda, Mozambique). SG4, SG5 [NAT/INST]
Outcome 3: The capacity of the private sector to participate in the production, marketing and trade of legal timber has increased
In both VPA and non-VPA countries, the FLEGT programme has effectively build capacity of private sector stakeholders and stimulated their engagement in in the timber value chain. The programme targeted specifically MSMEs through strengthening their associations. According to the 2020 annual report a total of 123 associations received support and 42 associations became formalized in 13 countries.
- In Indonesia, the MSMEs are deemed one of the stakeholders that are highly impacted by the requirements of the timber legality assurance system. In Cameroon, a total of 20 MSME associations were strengthened, of which 18 were formalized through programme support. The programme also worked with small timber consumers in cities who have had great difficulty in obtaining legal wood supply. This included artisanal wood workers to access legal timber. In Côte dIvoire, the programme raised awareness among the artisans of the need to preserve the forest cover and increase the notion of legal timber. Thanks to the support of the programme, one organisation, AVSI, contributed to the formalisation of several hundred artisanal carpenters. AVSI also managed to ensure that small operators could participate in the work of the larger private sector college, including in VPA negotiations. SG3, SG4 SG5 [ACT/TARGET]
- Through improved systems, training, access to markets and inclusion in platforms, private sector aactors have been formalized, obtained improved governance, have a stronger/better role in associations, with capacity and ability to continue actions post-project. Also, some show more inclusiveness and a broader scope (forest sector beyond timber sector). SG3 [ACT/TARGET]
Outcome 4: Stakeholders in both consumer and producer countries demonstrate an improved knowledge of benefits from legal logging, international trade requirements and of best practices for FLEGT
As part of global efforts to combat illegal logging and associated trade, demand-side measures have focused on trade regulations for wood products, requiring importers to apply due diligence to ensure the legality of their sources. Public and private sector organizations have also increased their commitment to legal and sustainable wood value chains by adopting corresponding procurement policies, international standards, and best practices. The FLEGT Action Plan (AP) combined these demand-side measures with the development of binding trade agreements - VPAs - between EU and tropical timber-producing countries. Central to the VPA was the development and implementation of national TLAS. A fully functional TLAS allowed tropical timber-producing countries to issue FLEGT licenses that can fulfil due diligence requirements for importers looking to introduce FLEGT-licensed timber products into the EU market.
- During Phase III of the Programme, one country (Indonesia) only started to issue FLEGT licences. SG4, SG5, SG3 [NAT/INST] [GLOB/NORM]
- FLEGT has produced 139 technical publications, through 46 projects at national, regional and global level. These cover many thematic issues, including national VPA/FLEGT processes, manuals for legality compliance, private sector situational assessments, market studies, REDD and FLEGT synergies and sustainable procurement. For instance, in Indonesia the programme has communicated emerging success stories and lessons learned through the publication of policy briefs, such as the policy briefs on the IFM case in Indonesia and the engagement of women in forest monitoring. The programme achieved effective knowledge sharing at national, regional and international level. FLEGT contributed to international events that stimulate South-South collaboration. Furthermore, the programme actively promoted exchange of experiences among different FLEGT countries and four out of six interviewed service providers mentioned benefits of regional exchange. [ACT/TARGET]
- At country level, communications did achieve to influence particular audiences. The FAO FLEGT team paid specific attention to increasing service providers communication skills that resulted effective. For instance, the Ghanian NGO Ecocare has worked with the private sector, civil society and government to prepare them to effectively communicate Ghanas FLEGT VPA processes, milestones and outcomes towards European Union market actors and other stakeholders, in preparation towards FLEGT licensing. SG4, SG5 [NAT/INST]
Outcome 5: The progress, achievements and impacts of the FLEGT Action Plan are better understood and information is made available through an updated, robust and user-friendly information system
Outcome 5 was added to the programme during implementation of FLEGT III, essentially to accommodate impact assessments of the FLEGT VPA process at country level, executed by CIFOR and ADE. Impact was considered from the entire FLEGT VPA process and is broader than the FLEGT programme, particularly because jobs and employment are not directly targeted by the programme and law enforcement is in part under control of governmental agencies. The four thematic areas in CIFOR/ADEs methodology for impact assessment are a selection of the seven measures of the FLEGT Action Plan. For outcome 5, it is assessed that together with CIFOR and ADE, FLEGT III managed to increase the understanding on the achievements and impacts of the FLEGT Action Plan in some VPA countries.
Outcome 6: Increased technical and institutional capacities of service providers
The programme supported approximately 200 service providers in the 17 countries.
- Increased capacities of service providers (CSOs, government agencies, research institutes, private sector associations). Through their participation in the FLEGT programme, service providers have received training and operative support for project development and execution. Through inclusion in stakeholder platforms, they have been empowered to participate in the value chain and decision making. The increase of technical and institutional capacities has been one of the most appreciated aspects of the programme, as evidenced by the evaluation e-survey: 85 percent of respondents find that there has been a moderate or significant positive change in capacity development of their own organizations, and institutional strengthening and/or improved capacity was the most frequently mentioned result that was generated through the FLEGT financial support. SG3 [NAT/INST]
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
